title: A blessed childhood – without indoor plumbing
text:
A blessed childhood – without indoor plumbing
At first glance, Meghan Cox Gurdon’s “Free Range Girl” might seem like the latest entry in an already crowded field of memoirs about painful childhoods. As a daughter of divorced parents who had little money, she ended up in a house without electricity, running hot water, or an indoor bathroom.
But as “Free Range Girl” unfolds, readers quickly grasp a brighter, warmer tone beneath the basics of Gurdon’s unusual 1970s upbringing in rural New England. “Looking back, though, I wouldn’t trade my experiences in Maine for anything – not for all the indoor plumbing in the world,” she writes.
Some years after Gurdon’s parents ended their marriage, they agreed that Gurdon should go live with her father in the farm country of Maine. His rustic life on a homestead lit by kerosene lanterns was, just like the rooms he’d built by hand, a product of his own design. A former technical writer for General Electric, he’d turned his back on corporate life. “Like tens of thousands of idealistic Americans in the 1970s, my father decided to renounce modern comforts and conveniences and go ‘back to the land,’” Gurdon recalls. “What this promised him, in theory, was an exhilarating life of greater simplicity, authenticity, and independence. What it delivered, in reality, was exhilaration plus a lot of hard work banging nails, cutting firewood, and tending animals.”
A renowned culture writer fondly reflects on how a rustic upbringing in rural Maine, with all its challenges and celebrations, shaped her as a person.
Even so, Gurdon came to cherish her new surroundings. “Dad’s house didn’t seem primitive to me,” she notes. “It was cozy.”
On her modest bookshelf, Gurdon already had useful models of self-sufficiency. “A Tree Grows in Brooklyn,” Betty Smith’s classic novel about a plucky young heroine with few resources but lots of smarts, was a favorite. The Laura Ingalls Wilder novels and E.B. White’s “Charlotte’s Web” were “worn and speckled from rereading,” too.
In her delight with the printed word, readers get an early glimpse of the woman Gurdon became. These days, after a long stint reviewing children’s books for The Wall Street Journal, she continues to write about culture for the newspaper. Her earlier book, “The Enchanted Hour,” celebrated the joy of reading aloud. Along with empowering her worldview, Smith and White also seemed to shape Gurdon’s prose style. It’s light and luminous, with turns of phrase that sparkle from the page like sun glinting from a New England snowscape.
Walking home in the winter dark, she wonders if she should be “exalted by the strangeness and wonder of the night” or scared of it. An owl appears and settles the question. “In its silent grandeur it allowed me to choose beauty over fear. I felt strong and serene all the way back to the house, almost as if I’d been blessed.”
Other blessings arrive. An extended family of uncles, aunts, and grandparents, sometimes drawn with a lightly comic touch, help Gurdon thrive. The tiny new school where she was once a lonely stranger elects her campus president. Electricity comes to her household – and with it, television and its tidings of the 1970s.
In the tradition of Susan Allen Toth’s “Blooming” and Bill Geist’s “Lake of the Ozarks,” this is a memoir of youth that spills treasures from its time capsule with casual abandon. Those who grew up a half a century ago will nod in recognition as young Gurdon watches “Gunsmoke,” adopts a Dorothy Hamill haircut, boogies to the beat of Peter Frampton, and quenches her thirst with Tang, “the drink of astronauts!” For younger readers, Gurdon offers a helpful tutorial on how a typewriter worked.
In the era evoked in “Free Range Girl,” popular culture helped form young minds but did not, like the internet to come, inhabit every corner of private life. “Life in 1976 was tactile, physical, and unfiltered,” Gurdon writes. “There were no smooth screens or glowing icons, only mechanical knobs to twist or buttons to push and, in Maine, latches to lift and logs to split and burn.”
Gurdon’s memoir will invite many readers to reflect on their own parenting styles, a hot topic as a national conversation continues to unfold about the line between raising youngsters and micromanaging them. But Gurdon doesn’t hold up the caprices and improvisations of her childhood as either a model or a cautionary tale. “Raising my family, I tried to imbue my children with the kind of self-reliance that comes from being free and taking risks,” she writes, “and I think I had some success, but the world was very different by then and independence came with a measure of anxiety.”
To read her book is to be reminded that childhood can be a puzzling passage for anyone, even in an ostensibly simpler time and place. Gurdon’s New England upbringing a half a century ago wasn’t always an idyll, but it was, at the very least, memorable.
“E.B. White said that he’d rather be unhappy in Maine than happy anywhere else,” she writes, “and I can’t say I disagree.”
